items.passage:
Calligraphy conservation is the specialized practice of stabilizing brushed ink manuscripts so that their strokes remain legible over centuries. The difficulty lies in the materials themselves. Traditional carbon inks sit on the surface of paper rather than binding chemically to it, and the animal glue that holds the pigment in place grows brittle as it ages. [■] Humidity swings then lift flakes of ink away, erasing the thin tapering ends of each stroke that carry the writer's hand.

These losses prompted conservators to develop consolidants, dilute adhesives that are brushed beneath lifting ink to re-anchor it. [■] The most effective formulations use polysaccharides derived from seaweed, which penetrate the paper fibers without darkening them or leaving a gloss. [■] Application demands extraordinary control, since one excess drop can spread through the sheet and blur the strokes the treatment is meant to preserve.

Despite this precision, consolidation remains imperfect. Treated manuscripts regain structural stability, yet the refractive index of the added polymer subtly alters how light scatters off the ink, flattening the tonal depth that distinguishes a master's brushwork from a copyist's. [■] Researchers are continuously uncovering how different consolidants age over decades, measuring color shift and stroke definition in treated samples to identify which formulations preserve not merely the mark but its character.

questions.stem: The word "brittle" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to

options.A: flexible
options.B: sticky
options.C: fragile
options.D: transparent

questions.explanation: The passage says the animal glue "grows brittle as it ages," after which humidity "lift[s] flakes of ink away" — the glue has become easily broken, that is, fragile.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what makes seaweed-derived consolidants effective?

options.A: They soak into the paper without adding color or shine.
options.B: They bond chemically with carbon ink on contact.
options.C: They can be applied in far larger quantities than glue.
options.D: They restore the original flexibility of aged paper.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states these formulations "penetrate the paper fibers without darkening them or leaving a gloss" — they enter the paper without altering color or adding shine.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about judging whether a consolidation treatment has succeeded?

options.A: It can be settled reliably as soon as the sheet dries.
options.B: Its full cost to the manuscript may emerge only much later.
options.C: It depends mainly on the skill of the original calligrapher.
options.D: It is more straightforward on manuscripts with thicker ink.

questions.explanation: Researchers must measure "color shift and stroke definition" as consolidants "age over decades," implying the damage a treatment causes is not apparent at the time of treatment.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the difference between a master's brushwork and a copyist's in paragraph 3?

options.A: To argue that copied manuscripts have little scholarly value.
options.B: To explain why brittle animal glue was replaced by modern polymers.
options.C: To identify which manuscripts should be treated first.
options.D: To show what is lost even when a treatment succeeds structurally.

questions.explanation: The contrast follows "Treated manuscripts regain structural stability, yet..." — it illustrates the cost of an otherwise successful treatment, namely the flattening of tonal depth.

questions.stem: There are four locations [■] in the passage that indicate where the following sentence could be added. 'And because that flattening is invisible under ordinary gallery lighting, curators may certify a treatment as successful long before its cost to the work becomes apparent.' Where would the sentence best fit? Select a location to add the sentence to the passage.

options.A: Slot 1 [■]
options.B: Slot 2 [■]
options.C: Slot 3 [■]
options.D: Slot 4 [■]

questions.explanation: The sentence opens with "that flattening," a back-reference to the tonal flattening described immediately before slot 4, and it sets up the closing point that researchers must track treated samples for decades.

items.passage:
Solution caves are underground voids formed when slightly acidic groundwater dissolves soluble bedrock, most commonly limestone. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and from soil, producing a weak carbonic acid that seeps along joints and bedding planes in the rock. [■] Over tens of thousands of years these narrow fractures widen into passages large enough for water to flow freely, and the rate of dissolution accelerates once that flow becomes turbulent.

This transition from slow seepage to open flow marks the beginning of a cave's mature phase. [■] Once the water table drops below a passage, the chamber drains and air replaces water, allowing a second process to begin: dripping water saturated with dissolved calcite loses carbon dioxide to the cave air and deposits a thin ring of mineral at each drip point. [■]

These deposits accumulate into the stalactites and stalagmites that characterize decorated caves. Their growth rate depends on how often water drips and on how much calcite it carries, so a single formation can preserve a legible record of surface climate stretching back hundreds of thousands of years. [■] Refinements in dating such layers promise even more precise reconstructions of past rainfall than field geologists once thought obtainable.

questions.stem: The word "saturated" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to

options.A: loaded
options.B: heated
options.C: stirred
options.D: filtered

questions.explanation: The water is "saturated with dissolved calcite" and then deposits that mineral, so it is carrying as much dissolved material as it can hold — loaded.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 1, what produces the weak acid that dissolves limestone?

options.A: Minerals released as the bedrock slowly fractures under great pressure.
options.B: Turbulent flow scouring the walls of narrow joints.
options.C: Calcite deposited along bedding planes in the rock.
options.D: Carbon dioxide taken up by rainwater from air and soil.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that "rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and from soil, producing a weak carbonic acid."

questions.stem: According to the passage, all of the following are true EXCEPT

options.A: Dissolution speeds up once the water begins to flow turbulently.
options.B: Stalactites form while a passage is still full of water.
options.C: Cave passages begin as narrow fractures in the bedrock.
options.D: A formation's growth depends partly on drip frequency.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 specifies that mineral deposition begins only after "the chamber drains and air replaces water," so the passage must be empty, not flooded.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about a formation that grew unusually quickly?

options.A: It must have formed while the passage was still flooded.
options.B: It likely records a period of heavier surface rainfall.
options.C: It contains less calcite than a slow-growing formation.
options.D: It cannot be dated by the methods geologists now use.

questions.explanation: Growth rate "depends on how often water drips," and the layers "preserve a legible record of surface climate" — faster growth therefore points to wetter conditions above.

questions.stem: There are four locations [■] in the passage that indicate where the following sentence could be added. 'For example, a drip arriving once a minute may leave a deposit only a fraction of a millimeter thick in a year.' Where would the sentence best fit? Select a location to add the sentence to the passage.

options.A: Slot 1 [■]
options.B: Slot 2 [■]
options.C: Slot 3 [■]
options.D: Slot 4 [■]

questions.explanation: The sentence is a concrete illustration of the drip-and-deposit mechanism just described at slot 3, and it prepares the reader for "These deposits accumulate" that opens the next paragraph.

items.passage:
Hydrogen bonding is an attraction between a hydrogen atom already bonded to a highly electronegative atom and a second electronegative atom nearby. Because oxygen, nitrogen, and fluorine pull shared electrons strongly toward themselves, the hydrogen they hold retains only a thin share of negative charge and takes on a partial positive one. [■] That exposed charge is what draws it toward a neighboring lone pair.

This attraction is far weaker than the covalent bond anchoring the hydrogen in place, yet its consequences are disproportionate. [■] In water, each molecule can take part in four such interactions at once, producing a fluctuating three-dimensional network that must be partly dismantled before the liquid can boil. [■] The high boiling point of water, long treated as an anomaly among comparable molecules, follows directly from the energy that dismantling requires.

Beyond simple liquids, the same interaction organizes biological structure. The two strands of a DNA double helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases, weak enough individually that an enzyme can peel them apart, numerous enough collectively that the molecule keeps its shape. [■] Despite the reach of this model, chemists still debate how much of the attraction is genuinely electrostatic and how much reflects partial covalent character.

questions.stem: The word "anomaly" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to

options.A: requirement
options.B: estimate
options.C: exception
options.D: tradition

questions.explanation: Water's boiling point is described as an anomaly "among comparable molecules" — it departs from what similar substances do, making it an exception.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 1, why does the hydrogen atom carry a partial positive charge?

options.A: It forms a lone pair with a neighboring atom.
options.B: It gains extra electrons from fluorine and nitrogen.
options.C: It sits between two covalent bonds at the same time.
options.D: Its shared electrons are pulled away by an electronegative partner.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 explains that oxygen, nitrogen, and fluorine "pull shared electrons strongly toward themselves," leaving the hydrogen with "a partial positive one."

questions.stem: What does "That exposed charge" refer to in paragraph 1?

options.A: The partial positive charge on the hydrogen atom
options.B: The negative charge held by oxygen or nitrogen
options.C: The lone pair on the neighboring atom
options.D: The shared electrons of the covalent bond

questions.explanation: The preceding sentence ends by saying the hydrogen "takes on a partial positive one," and that charge is what attracts the hydrogen to a nearby lone pair.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the hydrogen bonds holding DNA together?

options.A: They are stronger than the covalent bonds within each strand.
options.B: They must all break at once for the helix to open.
options.C: Their usefulness depends on being individually easy to break.
options.D: They occur only between oxygen and fluorine atoms.

questions.explanation: The passage stresses that the bonds are "weak enough individually that an enzyme can peel them apart" while still holding the shape collectively — the weakness is what makes the structure workable.

questions.stem: There are four locations [■] in the passage that indicate where the following sentence could be added. 'And because a single molecule can form several of them simultaneously, the weakness of any one is offset by sheer number.' Where would the sentence best fit? Select a location to add the sentence to the passage.

options.A: Slot 1 [■]
options.B: Slot 2 [■]
options.C: Slot 3 [■]
options.D: Slot 4 [■]

questions.explanation: The sentence explains the claim made immediately before slot 2 — that a weak attraction has disproportionate consequences — and introduces the multiplicity that the following sentence quantifies as "four such interactions at once."

items.passage:
Habit formation is the process by which a repeated behavior becomes triggered automatically by its setting rather than by deliberate decision. Early in learning, an action is guided by the reward it is expected to bring: a person walks to a particular cafe because they anticipate the coffee. With repetition in a stable context, control gradually shifts, and the cue itself, the route or the hour, becomes enough to launch the sequence.

This shift is mirrored by a change in which brain regions carry the behavior. Activity that begins in circuits tracking the value of outcomes migrates toward regions encoding the action sequence itself, a transfer that makes performance faster and less effortful. The trade-off is sensitivity: once the behavior is stamped in, devaluing the reward has surprisingly little immediate effect on whether the action still occurs.

These findings explain why habits resist simple resolutions to change. Because the controlling signal is the cue rather than the goal, deciding that an outcome is no longer desirable leaves the trigger fully intact. Interventions that succeed tend to work on the environment instead, removing or altering the cue so the sequence is never launched, and a habit's strength is best measured by how reliably the setting produces the act.

questions.stem: The word "devaluing" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to

options.A: discounting
options.B: repeating
options.C: delaying
options.D: concealing

questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts the reward's earlier importance with a state in which it matters less, so devaluing means treating the reward as worth less — discounting it.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what accompanies the shift toward automatic performance?

options.A: A steady rise in the measured value of the reward.
options.B: A slowing of the action as it becomes more precise.
options.C: A return of control to circuits that track outcomes.
options.D: A move of activity toward regions encoding the sequence.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that activity "migrates toward regions encoding the action sequence itself," which is what makes performance faster and less effortful.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about someone trying to break a habit?

options.A: They should concentrate on wanting the outcome less.
options.B: Changing their surroundings is likely to help more.
options.C: They will succeed once the behavior becomes effortful.
options.D: The habit will fade on its own in a stable context.

questions.explanation: Since deciding the outcome is undesirable "leaves the trigger fully intact" and successful interventions "work on the environment instead," altering the setting is the effective route.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention walking to a particular cafe in paragraph 1?

options.A: To show that habits are confined to everyday routines.
options.B: To contrast human habits with those of other animals.
options.C: To illustrate goal-directed action before a habit forms.
options.D: To explain why some cues are stronger than others.

questions.explanation: The example appears under "Early in learning, an action is guided by the reward it is expected to bring," so it depicts behavior still driven by the goal rather than by the cue.

questions.stem: According to the passage, all of the following are true EXCEPT

options.A: Repetition in a stable setting strengthens control by cues.
options.B: Automatic performance takes less effort than early learning.
options.C: Losing interest in a reward quickly ends the behavior.
options.D: Habit strength is gauged by how reliably a setting works.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says devaluing the reward "has surprisingly little immediate effect on whether the action still occurs," which directly contradicts this statement.

items.passage:
Curtailment is the deliberate reduction of output from a renewable generator at moments when the grid cannot absorb everything it could produce. Wind and solar installations deliver power according to the weather rather than demand, and on mild, bright, windy days their combined output can exceed what customers are drawing. Because electricity must be consumed the instant it is generated, operators order some plants to throttle back.

This mismatch between generation and demand has made storage central to renewable planning. Batteries absorb surplus midday output and release it after sunset, shifting energy across hours rather than days, while pumped hydroelectric storage moves water uphill into a reservoir and recovers most of that energy later through turbines. Each technology is defined less by how much it holds than by how long it can hold that energy economically.

Duration in turn determines which problems a given system can solve. A four-hour battery smooths the daily solar cycle but cannot cover a week of still, overcast weather, which is why planners increasingly pair short-duration storage with transmission lines reaching regions whose weather is uncorrelated with their own. Utilities now apply this reasoning when siting new capacity, treating a distant wind farm and a local battery as complementary rather than competing investments.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: The engineering behind pumped hydroelectric reservoirs.
options.B: Why electricity cannot be stored on a large scale.
options.C: How storage duration shapes responses to renewable oversupply.
options.D: The weather conditions that produce the most wind power.

questions.explanation: The passage moves from the oversupply problem that forces curtailment, to storage as the response, to duration as the property that decides which storage solves which problem.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 1, why must operators sometimes reduce renewable output?

options.A: Electricity has to be used at the moment it is produced.
options.B: Wind plants wear out faster when they run continuously.
options.C: Solar panels lose efficiency during mild, bright weather.
options.D: Customers tend to draw the most power on bright, windy days.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that "electricity must be consumed the instant it is generated," which is why operators order plants to throttle back when output exceeds demand.

questions.stem: How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?

options.A: It refines the distinction paragraph 2 draws between storage types.
options.B: It challenges the claim that storage is central to planning.
options.C: It supplies historical background for paragraph 2's technologies.
options.D: It restates paragraph 2's argument using a different example.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 ends by defining storage technologies by how long they hold energy; paragraph 3 opens with "Duration in turn determines..." and develops that criterion into practical siting decisions.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about long transmission lines?

options.A: They cost less to build than a four-hour battery system.
options.B: They can substitute for storage the grid would otherwise need.
options.C: They work best between regions with identical weather.
options.D: They remove any need to curtail renewable output at all.

questions.explanation: Because a short-duration battery "cannot cover a week of still, overcast weather," pairing it with lines to regions of uncorrelated weather supplies what longer storage would otherwise have to provide.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what distinguishes one storage technology from another?

options.A: The total volume of water each is able to move uphill.
options.B: Whether they release their energy before or after sunset.
options.C: The number of turbines needed to recover the energy.
options.D: How long they can economically retain the energy stored.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that each technology "is defined less by how much it holds than by how long it can hold that energy economically."
